Statement of the problem: The LGU, with the Provincial Government and the DOH, will build a 300-bed Level-3 general hospital as a regional referral center, teaching and training hospital and disaster-response facility, offering emergency, outpatient, inpatient, diagnostic, surgical, specialty and critical care, plus residency training, research and simulation. It uses a podium-and-tower scheme: a Central Podium (public, diagnostic, treatment, procedural, administrative and academic functions) with Tower A (adult inpatient) and Tower B (specialty inpatient: pediatric, OB, isolation, step-down), allowing expansion without disrupting operations. It must comply with the NBC, the Fire Code, BP 344, DOH Level-3 licensing standards and local zoning.

Site: a 50,000 m² government-owned lot. The southern frontage (main road) is for public entry, OPD and visitors; the eastern barangay road is for service, logistics and loading; the western parcel is reserved for future expansion. Amihan winds come from the northeast; there is strong western afternoon sun; noise comes from traffic on the southern road. Flood risk is low to moderate. Public, emergency (dedicated ambulance route) and service traffic are separated. Building footprint about 17,500 m², organized around a Central Healing Garden between the podium and the two towers.

Zoning and planning logic: public zone at the main entrance with direct access to OPD; emergency zone with separate ambulance access, direct access to surgery and ICU and immediate adjacency to imaging; critical care next to the surgical suite and close to imaging and ER; a sterile surgical zone with a direct relationship to CSSD; inpatient wards in the quietest part of the site, oriented north or east toward the healing garden; service and support on the east side with dirty traffic kept off sterile routes. Separate public, patient, bed, staff, service, clean, dirty and sterile circulation; two remote exits per floor, smoke-proof stairs, fire compartments, sprinklers, fire detection and a fire command center.

q: To support patient recovery, reduce stress, and maximize the therapeutic value of the inpatient environment, how should patient wards ideally be oriented?
o: Facing the streets to provide visual stimulation and connection to community life
Facing a landscaped arrival court to provide daylight, visual interest, and opportunities for observation
Facing an active public plaza to encourage social interaction and reduce patients' sense of isolation
Facing the healing garden to provide continuous views of vegetation, therapeutic landscapes, and natural elements
n: Views of vegetation and nature reduce stress and speed recovery. Wards should therefore face the healing garden. Source: Ulrich, "View through a window may influence recovery from surgery" (Science, 1984); design brief.

s: Project 5 – Rural Bank in Sta. Rosa (Adaptive Reuse)
q: The architect is tasked to convert the existing 1970s residence into a functional rural bank while preserving its character-defining features. Which architectural intervention best describes this process?
o: Restoration
Rehabilitation
Adaptive Reuse
Renovation
n: Converting a building to a new use while keeping its character is adaptive reuse. Restoration returns it to a past state, and renovation or rehabilitation updates it for its existing use. Source: Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013), Art. 1; NCCA/NHCP heritage guidelines.
scenario:
PROJECT NO. 5 – A PROPOSED RURAL BANK IN STA. ROSA, LAGUNA

Statement of the problem: A Filipino banker returning after 25 years in Hong Kong, Singapore and other ASEAN financial hubs will open a community-oriented rural bank for local entrepreneurs, farmers, industrial workers and small family businesses. He owns a 2-storey family house built in 1972 along a secondary road near the town center: reinforced concrete with adobe accents and Narra woodwork, large windows, terrazzo floors and a deep front setback. The architect must adaptively reuse it as the bank's main branch, complying with BSP requirements, security and vault standards, BP 344, the Fire Code, the NBC and local zoning, while preserving its 1970s character. Character-defining features to retain where feasible: adobe perimeter fence and wall accents, steel casement windows, terrazzo flooring, Narra woodwork (including the staircase), the covered ground-floor lanai facing the garden, mature landscaping, and the gable roof (originally clay tiles) with wide eaves.

Site: a 15.00 m × 30.00 m lot in a mixed residential-commercial district; the south boundary fronts a 10-m barangay road; residences to the north and east, a small commercial building to the west. 5.00-m front setback (to become customer and staff parking plus an armored-vehicle loading area) and 3.00-m rear setback (staff circulation, service and utilities). The former master bedroom becomes the Bank Manager's Office; the lanai keeps its link to the garden; a 24/7 ATM goes near the front with natural surveillance, CCTV and security lighting.

Objectives: full BP 344 compliance (accessible entrance, ramp, accessible toilet, accessible route to all public banking functions); clear separation of public banking, VIP and staff-only secured areas; a warm, familiar home character projecting stability and trust with earth tones and natural materials; contemporary interventions kept visually subordinate to the original house.

q: Which sequence BEST reflects the preferred conservation and adaptive reuse approach when evaluating existing building components?
o: Repair → Retain → Replace → Upgrade
Retain → Repair → Upgrade → Replace
Upgrade → Replace → Repair → Retain
Replace → Upgrade → Repair → Retain
n: Conservation practice goes from least to most intervention: retain first, then repair, upgrade, and replace only as a last resort. Source: Burra Charter (2013), Art. 3 (cautious approach); US Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation.
